title: Larkspur Air Route Profitability
prompt: Our client is Larkspur Air, a US regional airline. Larkspur flies from its hub airport to six mid-sized cities, using a fleet of identical 80-seat regional jets. It sells tickets mainly through its own website. Two years ago, in FY2023, Larkspur earned an operating profit of $20 million on $200 million of revenue. In FY2025, revenue was $176 million and the airline posted an operating loss of $4 million — even though its planes are about as full as they were before. Larkspur's CEO has asked us to figure out what caused the swing from profit to loss, and how the airline can get back to an operating profit within the next 12 months.
interviewerNotes: Source: AI Casing Case 02 (v1.0, Oct 2026), interviewer-led mode. Key insight: revenue and operating profit both fell $24M, so costs didn't move — it's a revenue problem, concentrated on Hub–Lakeport (−$9.6M) and Hub–Port Avery (−$14.4M); the other four routes net to zero. A low-cost airline entered those two routes early in FY2024 and Larkspur matched its fares: planes stayed 75% full but the Lakeport fare fell 40% ($200 → $120), so a Lakeport flight went from +$4,200 to −$600 of contribution (60 passengers × ($120 + $20 extras) − $9,000). Breakeven fare is $130 (above the $120 market), and the competitor's cost per seat is ~30% lower — Larkspur can't win a fare war. Those were its most profitable routes (~55% of FY2023 contribution on ~36% of flights). Fix: move the 5,000 flights to two uncontested new routes: 56 × $200 − $9,200 = +$2,000 per flight, +$10.0M a year, +$11.8M vs. today's −$1.8M on the contested routes, so operating profit ≈ +$7.8M at run rate (leases are fixed through 2030). Risk: at a 60% first-year load factor it's +$400 per flight and operating profit ≈ −$0.2M — phase the move and add supporting levers. Release order in the guide: Exhibit 1 (route results) → Exhibit 2 (Lakeport per-flight economics) → Exhibit 3 (new-route planning estimates, only after contribution per flight is calculated). If the candidate hasn't asked why fares fell by the end of the per-flight module, give the competitor entry before the network fix.

dataLedger.value: On the other four routes revenue and contribution stayed nearly flat: Hub–Cedar Bluff (2,500 flights) went from $38.0M to $38.4M of revenue and $5.0M to $5.4M of contribution; Hub–Granite Falls (2,500 flights) from $34.0M to $33.8M and $4.6M to $4.4M; Hub–Millbrook (2,000 flights) from $30.0M to $29.8M and $4.4M to $4.2M; and Hub–Westhaven (2,000 flights) held at $24.8M of revenue and $3.8M of contribution.

dataLedger.value: Across all six routes, revenue fell from $200.0M to $176.0M and contribution fell from $40.0M to $16.0M, on 14,000 flights a year — the same number of flights in both years.

dataLedger.value: Fixed costs — aircraft leases, hub facilities and corporate overhead — were $20.0M in both FY2023 and FY2025.

dataLedger.value: The low-cost airline's cost per seat is about 30% lower than Larkspur's — it flies larger planes and has lower labor costs — and its fares are about the same as Larkspur's current fares.

dataLedger.label: Connecting passengers on the contested routes

dataLedger.label: New routes (Hub–Ashford, Hub–Brookhaven): seats, load factor, fare and extras
dataLedger.value: The planning estimate for the two new routes, Hub–Ashford and Hub–Brookhaven, is 80 seats per flight, a 70% load factor, a $180 average one-way fare and $20 of extras per passenger.

dataLedger.label: New routes: variable cost per flight and flights per year
dataLedger.spoken: the new routes' costs and flights
dataLedger.value: Variable cost on the new routes is estimated at $9,200 per flight, across 5,000 flights a year that would use the aircraft time freed by exiting Hub–Lakeport (2,000 flights) and Hub–Port Avery (3,000 flights).

dataLedger.label: New routes: competition and fixed costs
dataLedger.spoken: the new routes' competition and fixed costs

structureKey: A strong structure builds an airline profit tree — revenue = passengers (seats × load factor) × revenue per passenger (fare + extras), by route; variable costs per flight (fuel, crew, maintenance, airport and landing fees); fixed costs (aircraft leases, hub, overhead); and external changes (competition, demand, fuel). Strong candidates use the clue that revenue and profit both fell $24M (so costs didn't move — it's revenue), link 'planes as full as before' to a lower fare, want to look route by route, and hypothesize a new competitor or fare war on specific routes. Red flags: generic frameworks with no link to profit, most of the answer on cost cutting, an unprioritized list, ignoring the route dimension.
recommendationKey: The loss has one cause: a low-cost competitor entered Larkspur's two most profitable routes (Hub–Lakeport and Hub–Port Avery) in FY2024. Larkspur matched fares to keep its passengers, so its planes stayed just as full, but fares fell 40% on Lakeport ($200 to $120); costs and flights didn't change, so the $24M revenue loss fell straight to the bottom line, and a Lakeport flight went from +$4,200 to −$600 of contribution. Larkspur can't win a fare war (breakeven fare $130 vs. $120; the competitor's cost per seat is ~30% lower). Recommendation: move those 5,000 flights a year to the two uncontested new routes — about +$11.8M a year and an operating profit of ~$7.8M at full run rate (leases are fixed, so exiting without redeploying saves only $1.8M). Key risk: new routes ramp up slowly — at a 60% first-year load factor Larkspur is only near breakeven — so phase the move (keep a reduced peak schedule on the contested routes or launch one new route first), protect the four remaining routes, and watch the ~20% connecting passengers and a competitor following onto the new routes.

answerKeyIdeas.idea: Keep a reduced peak-time schedule on the contested routes during ramp-up
Codeshare or interline with a larger airline to feed connecting passengers
Protect the four uncontested routes (loyalty, corporate contracts, schedule)
Sublease aircraft time to another airline during ramp-up
Renegotiate airport fees at the new stations
Pre-sell the new routes and market them to connecting passengers
